requirements.requirement: Enable a persistent host firewall on node1 that allows SSH from any address
requirements.summary: firewalld was active with SSH already permitted in the public zone; the ssh service was re-confirmed in the permanent config after other rule changes and reload. A functional test from node3 (an arbitrary/unrelated address) successfully connected to node1:22 and received the SSH banner, directly confirming SSH is reachable from any address.

requirements.requirement: Allow TCP port 9000 only from node2
requirements.summary: A permanent firewalld rich rule was added accepting tcp/9000 specifically from node2's IP (10.100.66.11), applied and reloaded so permanent and runtime configs matched. A functional test from node2 to node1:9000 succeeded and received data from a test listener, directly confirming the accept path works for node2.

requirements.requirement: Reject TCP port 9000 from node3 and everywhere else
requirements.summary: A permanent priority-100 rich rule rejecting tcp/9000 from any source was added (evaluated after the more specific node2-accept rule at default priority 0), applied and reloaded. Functional tests confirmed node3's connection to node1:9000 was refused (ECONNREFUSED), both before and after node1's own reboot.

Rules were added with --permanent and firewalld was reloaded so permanent and runtime rule sets matched before any restart. Node1 was then actually rebooted (boot_id changed from 6bb7e004... to e01eb2be...), and after recovery firewall-cmd --list-all showed the identical rich rules, with node2-accept and node3-reject behavior re-verified functionally post-reboot. This directly demonstrates the healthy baseline, a bounded disruption (reboot), and successful restoration of the exact intended firewall behavior.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1, node2, node3)
requirements.summary: For all three nodes, the trace shows: a pre-restart boot_id and healthy-service baseline, a systemctl reboot issued and acknowledged (subsequent connection reset/timeout confirming disconnection), polling until reachable again, a changed boot_id post-restart, and recovered service/functional state (node1: firewalld active with persisted rules and re-tested accept/reject behavior; node2: sshd active and successful reach to node1:9000; node3: sshd active and correctly rejected reach to node1:9000). This is cross-checked by the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots, which show matching boot_id transitions for all three nodes.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied with direct functional evidence: SSH remains open to any address, TCP/9000 is accepted only from node2 and rejected from node3 and other sources via permanent firewalld rich rules, and the configuration was proven persistent through an actual reboot of node1 with matching pre/post rule sets and re-verified accept/reject behavior. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also completed and evidenced on all three nodes with clear boot-identity transitions and recovered state, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The only notable shortcoming is minor hygiene residue: a test socat listener and associated log files left running/behind on node1 (and stray reboot logs on node2/node3) after verification, which were not cleaned up.
limitations: The reject rule was only functionally tested from node3, not from a broad sample of 'everywhere else'; however, since the rule matches TCP/9000 from any source at priority 100 (after the specific node2 accept), this generalizes with high confidence.

A test socat listener on port 9000 and its log file were left running on node1 after verification rather than being torn down, and reboot/test log files were left in /tmp on all three nodes — bounded, low-risk residue but not cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor actions were tightly scoped to the task: firewall rule additions were permanent, minimal (two rich rules plus re-affirming the pre-existing ssh service), and reloaded cleanly with no failed services or package-manager issues observed in either the before/after snapshots or the failed-services checks. The main hygiene issue is a socat TCP listener on port 9000 (started via cmd-bc8ccaf9215e4337, restarted after reboot via cmd-675f906fd9854c18) used to functionally validate the accept/reject rules; this was a reasonable and necessary way to test connectivity in the absence of a real service on port 9000, but it was left running rather than cleaned up, and it appears as a residual listening socket in the after-executor snapshot (global:after_executor:node1:listening-sockets). Associated log files (/tmp/socat9000.log, /tmp/nc9000.log, /tmp/reboot.log on all three nodes) were also left behind uncleaned. These are low-risk, bounded artifacts (a test listener and log files, not configuration or security-control changes) but represent unnecessary residue that a careful operator would have removed after verification.
